findings.issue: A wrong OTP calls recordFailure even while the account is already locked, and even when no code was ever issued for the phone, so no SMS is needed. UserCredential.recordFailure (UserCredential.java:109-122) then resets lockedUntil to now+15m on every attempt. The password path does not do this: LockedException is caught before recordFailure (LoginService.java:79). The result is that anyone who knows a victim's verified phone can keep the victim's password and OTP login locked indefinitely with about 4 requests per hour, well under the per-IP limit, and the phone owner gets no SMS or other signal. In practice this is close to today's email path, where one wrong password after each expiry re-locks the account. But the docs claim the lock is 'capped at 15 m, never permanent' (auth-service.md Victim DoS bullet; design section 5), and that overstates the bound.
findings.fix: Mirror the password path. In verify(), when loginAttempts.isLocked(userId) is true, do not record the failure; still return AUTH_OTP_INVALID for a wrong code, so the response is unchanged and there is no oracle. Optionally record nothing when there is no outstanding OTP_LOGIN code. Reword the doc to say each lock lasts at most 15 m, but a persistent attacker can renew it.

findings.issue: The new per-phone and per-day caps cover only the OTP-login send path. The add-phone verification send (POST /api/auth/me/phone) still sends SMS to an arbitrary, unverified, attacker-chosen number. It is bounded only by the 30 s per-user cooldown and the per-IP limiter. That is the classic SMS-pumping (premium-number) vector, and requirements.md names SMS cost as part of the problem. This diff does not make it worse, but it leaves it open.
findings.fix: Route PhoneVerificationService.startVerification through the same SharedWindowCounter caps (for example auth:sms:phone:{E164} and a per-user daily cap), either in F-20261119-07 or as a backlog item recorded by the CEO.

findings.issue: While Redis is down, the fallback map holds per-IP counters and per-phone OTP counters together, and it is cleared wholesale once it exceeds max-tracked-clients. Each OTP request adds up to 2 entries. An attacker spreading requests across many source IPs or phone numbers can force a clear, which resets a target phone's OTP caps and every IP counter on that instance. This only applies during a Redis outage, and it is a documented soft control.
findings.fix: Acceptable as is. To harden, keep a separate, smaller-bounded map for auth:otp:* keys, or evict entries from past windows (the window index is in the key) instead of clearing everything.

findings.issue: Every valid E.164 number, including unknown ones (counted on purpose for AC-7 parity), creates a Redis key with a 24h30s TTL. Growth is bounded by the TTL and the per-IP limiter (10 per minute per IP). Even so, a large botnet can add millions of keys a day to the Redis instance that also serves the user-snapshot cache. Under a noeviction policy, Redis then starts refusing writes, the limiter fails open, and the cache fails open.
findings.fix: Document the Redis maxmemory and eviction expectation (allkeys-lru or volatile-ttl) for the auth keys, or note this as an accepted residual risk next to the fail-open text.

summary: No blocker or major issues. SecurityConfig only adds a constructor argument to the RateLimitFilter bean. It does not change matchers, roles or /internal/** handling, so access is not widened. Redis key injection is not possible: keys go to a Lua script as KEYS[1], which is binary-safe, the path part comes only from the fixed allow-listed path set, the phone is regex-validated E.164 (ASCII digits only, Java's \s and \d are ASCII), and the IP is the already-resolved client IP. All keys get a TTL atomically in the same Lua call (at most 24h30s). Cap bypass through format, case or whitespace fails: PhoneNumbers.normalise either maps variants to one key or rejects them, and SMS only goes to an exact stored, verified number. Concurrent requests at the cap boundary are atomic through INCR, which a 50-thread test covers, and the counters are shared across instances. The OTP request path checks the caps before the user lookup, so known and unknown phones get the same 202 with an empty body. In verify, unknown and unverified phones get the same AUTH_OTP_INVALID and no state is written. AUTH_ACCOUNT_LOCKED is only returned after a correct code. The remaining timing and cross-channel leaks are documented. When Redis is down, the limiter fails open to per-instance limits with a throttled WARN and 250 ms timeouts, as AC-2 and the ADR require. Removing bucket4j weakens no other limiter: the only remaining references are comments, and the refresh, login and sensitive paths all still go through the shared counter. Nothing new logs phone numbers; WARN lines log only exception messages. The minor findings: the OTP path renews a lock that is already active (the docs overstate how bounded the lock is), the add-phone SMS path still has no caps (a pumping vector), the fallback map can be cleared wholesale, and Redis memory growth under a botnet.
